title: Wildfire
description: Use this list before fire season to harden your home, plan your exit, and protect your lungs from smoke - then leave early when fire threatens.

sources.title: When Smoke Is in the Air
Firewise USA Immediate Noncombustible Zone Fact Sheet
sources.publisher: Texas A&M Forest Service / NFPA Firewise

items.text: Learn your evacuation zone and sign up for county emergency alerts
Plan at least two ways out of your neighborhood and a meeting place outside the area
Leave as soon as you are told - or sooner if you feel unsafe; do not wait to see flames
Pack a go-bag for each person and pet and keep it by the door or in the car
Keep NIOSH-approved N95 respirators for every person - cloth masks and bandanas do not block smoke
Clear the first 5 feet (1.5 m) around the house of anything embers can ignite: mulch, leaves, firewood, doormats, woody shrubs
Clean roofs and gutters and cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh
Work outward to 100 feet (30 m): mow grass, space and trim trees and shrubs, remove dead plants
Arrange early help for anyone who cannot drive, and move livestock early - they need much more time
Practice leaving in 10 minutes with everyone and the pets
On red flag days, park facing out with a full tank and the go-bag inside
When fire is near: close windows, vents, and doors, leave doors unlocked, move patio furniture and cushions away, and turn on outside lights
Connect garden hoses but do not leave sprinklers running - it drains water pressure firefighters need
Wear long sleeves, long pants, and boots of cotton or wool when leaving
Know the trapped plan: call 911; in a car park away from plants, keep windows closed, and get low under a wool blanket
Set up a clean room with a portable air cleaner sized for the room - never an ozone generator
Keep MERV 13 filters for central air (or to build a box-fan air cleaner) for smoke days
Check the Air Quality Index on AirNow and limit time outdoors when it is high
Ask your fire department or state forestry agency about a free home wildfire assessment
After the fire, return only when officials say it is safe; children and people with heart or lung disease should not do ash cleanup
